system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

C. Template Language in 13 Additional Languages 12. We adopt the multilingual templates located in Appendix D. In the WEA Multilingual Public Notice, the Bureau proposed translations in Arabic, Chinese (Simplified), French, German, Haitian Creole, Hindi, Italian, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Tagalog, and Vietnamese, which were developed through a contracted professional translation service. In addition to the comments submitted into the record, the Bureau worked with the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau to acquire feedback from native language speakers and communities representing the populations these alerts are intended to reach. We received feedback on these templates from language teachers and members of local, state, and national organizations representing communities of language speakers. The comments we received were evaluated with the assistance of the Commission's contracted professional translation services. Based on this feedback, we adopt templates in the written forms of the 13 most commonly spoken languages in the United States after English. data.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning across the headline, description and instruction. The hazard is the same: rain from convective clouds (السحب الركامية), light to moderate and heavy at times. The day (Saturday), the times (13:30 to 21:00) and the areas (some eastern, southern and western areas and parts of the interior) all match. The protective action also matches: take care outdoors or while driving during rain, and follow official updates at the same URL. I found no difference in meaning. The Arabic was produced by machine translation, so a named person who reads Arabic must still review and approve it before release. I cannot approve it.
